title: Erdős Problem #931: Same Prime Factors in Products of Consecutive Integers
description: Let k₁ ≥ k₂ ≥ 3. Are there only finitely many n₂ ≥ n₁+k₁ such that ∏(n₁+i) and ∏(n₂+j) share the same prime factors? Counterexamples to the stronger claim exist (AlphaProof: 10! and 14·15·16). OPEN.

meta.author: Erdős
meta.assumptions: 2 axioms: stronger_implies_main (Størmer-type smooth number argument), exists_prime_between_blocks_hard (refined: only the hard case with k₁<n₁, tight gap, all factors ≤n₁ — general statement proved as theorem). overview.historicalContext: Erdős posed this problem in 1976 [Er76d], asking about the finiteness of pairs of consecutive-integer blocks whose products share the same set of prime factors. The problem appears in Guy's _Unsolved Problems in Number Theory_ as Problem B35. The question connects to deep themes in multiplicative number theory: the radical $\text{rad}(n)$ (product of distinct prime factors) of a product $(n+1)\cdots(n+k) = (n+k)!/n!$ depends on which primes $\leq n+k$ divide at least one element of the block. Erdős himself doubted the full conjecture and proposed the weaker claim that same-prime-factor pairs must satisfy $n_2 > 2(n_1 + k_1)$ with finitely many exceptions. This stronger conjecture was disproved by a counterexample: $10! = 2^8 \cdot 3^4 \cdot 5^2 \cdot 7$ and $14 \cdot 15 \cdot 16 = 2^5 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7$ share prime factors $\{2,3,5,7\}$ with $n_2 = 13 \leq 20 = 2(n_1 + k_1)$. Tijdeman found another example: $19 \cdot 20 \cdot 21 \cdot 22$ and $54 \cdot 55 \cdot 56 \cdot 57$ share the same primes (this one beyond the double gap). The connection to Bertrand's postulate is central: for $n_2 > 2(n_1 + k_1)$, a prime in $(n_1 + k_1, 2(n_1 + k_1)]$ would divide the second block but not the first, reducing the problem to the bounded-gap case. The constraint $k_1, k_2 \geq 3$ excludes trivial infinite families for small block sizes.
overview.problemStatement: Let $k_1 \geq k_2 \geq 3$. Are there only finitely many $n_2 \geq n_1 + k_1$ such that $\prod_{i=1}^{k_1}(n_1+i)$ and $\prod_{j=1}^{k_2}(n_2+j)$ have the same set of prime factors?
overview.text: Let k₁ ≥ k₂ ≥ 3. Are there only finitely many n₂ ≥ n₁+k₁ such that ∏(n₁+i) and ∏(n₂+j) share the same prime factors? Counterexamples to the stronger claim exist (AlphaProof: 10! and 14·15·16). OPEN.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization defines `consecutiveProduct` via `Finset.Icc` and `Finset.prod`, extracts prime factor sets via `Nat.primeFactors`, and defines `SamePrimeFactors` as equality of these Finsets. The main conjecture uses `Set.Finite` on the solution set. Both the stronger conjecture ($n_2 \leq 2(n_1+k_1)$) and the prime-between-blocks question are stated as axioms. Two counterexamples (AlphaProof and Tijdeman) are fully verified by `native_decide` and `omega`. Structural properties (positivity, prime factor membership, equivalence relation) are proved. The file uses 0 sorry statements; all deep results are axioms.
keyInsights: AlphaProof counterexample: $10!$ and $14 \cdot 15 \cdot 16$ share prime factors $\{2,3,5,7\}$ with $n_2 \leq 2(n_1+k_1)$, disproving the stronger conjecture
Tijdeman's example: $19 \cdot 20 \cdot 21 \cdot 22$ and $54 \cdot 55 \cdot 56 \cdot 57$ share primes but with $n_2 > 2(n_1+k_1)$, so the original finiteness question persists
Bertrand's postulate reduces the problem: for $n_2 > 2(n_1+k_1)$, a prime in $(n_1+k_1, 2(n_1+k_1)]$ provides a distinguishing factor, so only the bounded-gap case matters
The constraint $k_1, k_2 \geq 3$ is essential: for $k = 1$ or $k = 2$, infinitely many pairs trivially share prime factors (e.g., all even consecutive products share the prime 2)
Erdős could not prove even the subsidiary question: must a prime exist between $n_1$ and $n_2 + k_2$ when the blocks share prime factors?
The `SamePrimeFactors` relation is an equivalence relation on $(n, k)$ pairs, suggesting a quotient structure that could organize the solution space

sections.title: Verified Counterexamples
sections.summary: Five verified examples: AlphaProof (n₁=0, k₁=10, n₂=13, k₂=3), Tijdeman (n₁=18, k₁=k₂=4, n₂=53), and three new small examples showing {4,5,6}/{8,9,10}, {3,4,5,6}/{8,9,10}, and {1..5}/{8,9,10} share prime factors {2,3,5}. All verified by native_decide and omega.

sections.title: Properties of Prime Factors
sections.summary: Seven lemmas: prime factors divide the product and are prime, a prime dividing any n+i is in the factor set (via Finset.dvd_prod_of_mem), and SamePrimeFactors is reflexive, symmetric, transitive.

sections.title: Bertrand's Postulate and Prime Between Blocks
sections.summary: NEW: Four theorems using Bertrand's postulate. (1) If the first block contains a prime, a prime exists in range (trivial). (2) By Bertrand, when k₁ ≥ n₁ the first block always has a prime. (3) Combined: exists_prime_between_blocks holds for k₁ ≥ n₁ without SamePrimeFactors. (4) If the first product has a large prime factor, SamePrimeFactors transfers it to bound q ≤ n₂+k₂ via Prime.dvd_finset_prod_iff.

sections.title: Prime Between Blocks: Proved from Refined Axiom
sections.summary: The general exists_prime_between_blocks statement is now a THEOREM proved by 4-way case analysis: (1) k₁≥n₁ via Bertrand, (2) n₂+k₂≥2n₁ via Bertrand, (3) large prime factor transfer via SamePrimeFactors, (4) refined axiom for the hard case (k₁<n₁, tight gap, all factors ≤n₁). The hard-case axiom is strictly weaker than the original, with 3 additional hypotheses constraining when Størmer-type smooth number theory is needed.
sections.mathContext: The general exists_prime_between_blocks statement is now a THEOREM proved by 4-way case analysis. Only the hard case (k₁<n₁, n₂+k₂<2n₁, all prime factors ≤n₁) remains as an axiom. This case forces both blocks to be n₁-smooth, making it likely vacuously true by Størmer-type results.

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #931 asks whether two far-apart blocks of consecutive integers can share the same set of prime factors only finitely often. The formalization defines the core objects (`consecutiveProduct`, `consecutivePrimeFactors`, `SamePrimeFactors`), states the main finiteness conjecture and its stronger variant, and fully verifies two counterexamples to the stronger claim. Seven structural lemmas are proved (including the equivalence relation property), and the Bertrand's postulate reduction and prime-between-blocks question are recorded as axioms. The file uses 0 sorry statements.
conclusion.implications: Resolution would illuminate the multiplicative structure of consecutive integers at a deep level: how far apart can blocks be while sharing the exact same prime support? The connection to Bertrand's postulate and prime gaps means progress could come from improved bounds on prime distribution in structured intervals. The problem also connects to the abc conjecture (which constrains radical sizes in additive relations) and to Grimm's conjecture (which requires distinct prime factors for consecutive composite numbers).
openQuestions: Are there only finitely many pairs $(n_1, n_2)$ with same prime factors for fixed $k_1 \geq k_2 \geq 3$? The main conjecture remains completely open.
Must a prime exist between $n_1$ and $n_2 + k_2$ when blocks share prime factors? Even this seemingly weaker consequence is unproved.
What is the growth rate of the largest $n_2$ with $\text{SamePrimeFactors}(n_1, k_1, n_2, k_2)$ as a function of $n_1$ and $k$?
Are there infinitely many counterexamples to the stronger conjecture ($n_2 \leq 2(n_1+k_1)$), or is the AlphaProof example essentially isolated?
How does the problem change if we require not just the same prime factor set but the same prime factorization signature (same multiset of exponents)?
